title: The Blue Kestrel Journal
description: Marion Teale's memory site for the Blue Kestrel diner: the menus, the photographs, who sat in which booth, the 1977 fire, and an honest paragraph about the pie. Built 2002. Nothing new since 2019.

data.author: Marion Teale
data.tagline: a diner, written down while there was still somebody to ask
data.about:
I am Marion Teale. I waitressed at the Blue Kestrel from 1971 to 1979, mornings, and then I worked in the county clerk's office until I retired in 2012. Those two jobs are the same job. You write down what happened, you put it where somebody can find it, and you do not improve it.

I built this in 2002 on a program that came free with the computer. It puts the pictures where it wants to and I have stopped fighting it.

What is here: the menus I kept, the photographs I was given or took, the booth map, the 1977 fire with the date on it, and the fact about the pie. I am not a historian. I am a person who was there and who kept the paper.

If you want to correct me, write to me. My address is in the county directory and has not changed since 1981.

posts.title: why this is here
posts.body:
Hal Sowerby's daughter Doris called me in February to ask whether I still had a menu. I had four. She wanted to know what year hers was and I could tell her, because I had written the year on the back of mine in 1974 for no reason at all.

That is the whole argument for this. There are perhaps thirty people left who can say what the Blue Kestrel was actually like on a Tuesday morning, and we are all of an age where the number goes down and does not go up.

So: menus, photographs, the booth map, and anything anybody sends me that I can check. If I cannot check it I will say so in the same sentence.

The diner is still open. It is at 214 Mill Street in Gridfall and Ed Dombrowski still sits in the second booth from the door. I am not writing an obituary. I am writing it down while I can still ring somebody up and ask.

comments.author: marla
comments.body: Finally. I have been telling you to do this for two years. Putting you on my links page.

comments.author: Ed D.
comments.body: Marion called to ask permission. I said it is a diner, not a secret.

posts.title: the booth map
posts.body:
[img:photo:kestrel-booth-map-1974]

Six booths, eleven stools. That is the whole room and it has not changed since before I started.

I have drawn this the way you see it coming in the door, which is the only way anybody ever saw it.

[list][*][b]Booth one[/b], by the window. Salesmen, and anybody who wanted to be seen from the street. Nobody local sat there twice.
[*][b]Booth two[/b]. Ed's. He does his ordering there and he has done it there since 1978. If you sit in booth two he will not say anything and you will feel it anyway.
[*][b]Booth three[/b]. The Kesterke family every Sunday after nine o'clock mass, four of them, and later six.
[*][b]Booth four[/b]. Whoever. This is the only booth with no history and I have always thought that was restful.
[*][b]Booths five and six[/b], the two at the back. The retired county highway men, Tuesday mornings, from about 1980 onward. Before that it was the same men on the same morning, still working, in the same two booths, which I think is the best thing I know about this county.
[/list]

The stools were not anybody's. That is what a stool is for.

comments.author: W. Pennock
comments.body: Booth three is right. My mother would not sit anywhere else and she was not a woman who explained herself.

posts.title: the menus, and the one from 1974
posts.body:
[img:photo:kestrel-menu-1974-front]

I have four. 1971, 1974, 1983 and one that is either 1990 or 1991 because I did not write on that one and I have learned my lesson.

The 1974 is the one people ask for, and it is the one I wrote the year on the back of, on a Saturday in June, sitting in booth four before open. So I can date it exactly and I am insufferable about it.

[list][*]Two eggs any style, toast, potatoes — $1.15
[*]Two eggs with ham or sausage — $1.65
[*]Short stack — $0.95
[*]Coffee — $0.15, and refills were not counted or charged
[*]Pie — $0.35
[/list]

The coffee has been the same brand since at least 1980. Ed says that is not a boast, it is just true, and he is right, and he says it anyway.

The 1983 menu has a sandwich on it called the Kestrel Special which was ham, egg and a slice of tomato, and which lasted under a year. Nobody has ever asked me about it. I am putting it here so that it exists somewhere.

posts.title: they are taking it out to 62
posts.body:
The last plate on Mill Street went out on Sunday 22 August, after the breakfast service, and the food ran out around twenty past eleven which is exactly what Ed said would happen.

It is not closed. I want that said plainly at the top because the paper made it sound closed and then half the county rang each other up about it.

Hollis Property Group wanted a number Ed could not make on eggs. So he has taken it out to the old roadhouse building on County Route 62 in Ashkettle, at the Kestrel Road corner, and he opened there three weeks later with the same counter, the same six booths and, as far as I can tell, the same coffee.

What did not come: the sign. It is eleven feet long and it needs a pole and a transformer and neither of those things came out to 62 in August. It is in Ed's garage on Fenn Avenue. He says he could not get the car in.

The Tuesday men did not go out to 62. It is nine miles and most of them do not drive that far any more, so they took a vote — an actual vote, in booth five — and moved to the deli counter at Hollis Market, which several of them described to me as temporary. That was six weeks ago and it is still temporary.

214 Mill Street is empty as of this week. I have no photograph of it empty and I am not going to take one.

comments.author: marla
comments.body: I have the last week on Mill Street on film, all of it, and I will put it up when I can look at it.

posts.title: the photographs, and who is in them
posts.body:
[img:photo:kestrel-staff-1976-counter]

Eleven photographs so far. Most were given to me. Two are mine.

The one above is the counter in 1976 and I can name everybody in it, which will not be true for very much longer, so here they are in order from the left: Hal Sowerby, who founded it and who is in almost no pictures because he took almost all of them; Dot Wierzbicki, who did the baking and who is the reason for the post I am not writing yet; me, aged twenty-four and furious about something; and Ann Kesterke.

The man at the end with his back turned is not staff and I have never known who he is. Somebody will tell me and then I will have to change this.

If you have a photograph of the inside of that building at any date, I will scan it and give it straight back. I have a scanner now. My nephew set it up and wrote the steps on a card.

posts.title: it closed
posts.body:
The Blue Kestrel closed for good on Saturday 25 November 2006, out on Route 62, two years and three months after it left Mill Street.

The lease again. It is always the lease. Ed is sixty-five and he said the second one took more out of him than the first one and I believe him.

So: 1961 to 2006. Forty-five years, in two buildings, under two owners, with one coffee.

I went out on the Saturday. I had not meant to. There were more cars than the lot holds and people were parked along the shoulder facing the wrong way, and inside it was everybody who had not been in since about 1994, telling Ed how much they loved the place. I did not say the thing I wanted to say about that, and neither did Marla, and we agreed afterwards in the lot that we had both nearly said it.

I will keep adding to this site. There is more paper than there is time.

comments.author: Ed D.
comments.body: Marion. It was forty-five years and I am going to sleep until six. Thank you for the write up. You got the coffee right.

comments.author: dennis o.
comments.body: I was there Saturday. Never went in once in twelve years of driving past it. That is on me.

posts.title: the fire, with the date on it
posts.body:
This is the post I should have written first, because it is the thing the internet gets wrong about us.

[b]The kitchen fire was on Tuesday 8 March 1977.[/b] It started in the fryer, at about a quarter past five in the morning, before we opened. Ann Kesterke's husband Lou drove the 1968 Ford up from the Gridfall station and told that story the same way for thirty two years, which is how I know I have it right.

[b]It did not close the diner.[/b] We were open again eleven days later, on Saturday 19 March, on a griddle and a hot plate, with no fryer and a hand-lettered card in the window apologising for it. The card is in the folder. The fryer came back in May.

I am putting this in bold because I have now read in three separate places that the Blue Kestrel was destroyed by a fire in 1977, or closed after a fire in 1977, or burned down. It did not burn down. It closed in 2006 because of a lease, twenty-nine years later, in a different building, in a different town.

I do not know how to stop people saying it. I can only put the date here.

comments.author: W. Pennock
comments.body: Filed. This is the kind of page that is worth more than the ten that repeat each other.

posts.title: the pie was not good
posts.body:
People write to me about the pie. They have been writing to me about the pie since 2002 and they will write to me about it after I am done. So.

[b]The pie was not good.[/b]

It was not bad. It was a diner pie made in quantity by a woman with eleven other things to do, and Dot Wierzbicki would have told you so herself, because she did tell me so, in 1974, in those words, while making forty of them.

The crust was shortening and it was heavy. The apple was tinned after about 1972. The cherry was always tinned. What was good was that it was thirty-five cents and it was there at half past five in the morning when nothing else in this county was there at all, and you were eating it in a warm room with somebody who knew your name.

That is what people remember and they are not wrong to remember it. They have just attached it to the pie.

I have the recipe. It is four lines on a card in Dot's hand and I am not going to print it, because the one thing worse than a pie that was not good is forty people finding out at once.

comments.author: marla
comments.body: I have been waiting nine years for you to write this down.

comments.author: a reader
comments.body: This is the only honest sentence about a local restaurant I have ever read on the internet.

posts.title: there is a vape shop in it now
posts.body:
The Route 62 building has been empty since 2006 and as of this spring it is Kestrel Vapor, which sells electronic cigarettes.

I have had four letters about this and all four expected me to be upset. I am not upset. An empty building on a county route falls down. This one has a roof that is being looked at and a floor that is being swept and somebody in it during the day.

They kept the sign. They did not have a choice about keeping the sign, as I understand it, because a new one costs more than the lease and the old one is grandfathered under the county ordinance. But they kept it lit, and that they did have a choice about.

posts.title: the bird is not a kestrel
posts.body:
[img:photo:kestrel-neon-bird-night]

The sign is eleven feet long. It was made in 1968, the year the diner took the Blue Kestrel name, by a sign shop in Ardo that closed in 1991. Before 1968 it was Kestrel Creek Lunch, after the creek behind the Mill Street block.

The bird is not a kestrel.

It is not any bird. The shop in Ardo had a bird, and Hal Sowerby was shown the bird, and Hal Sowerby said fine. Every single person who has ever asked me about this site has asked me about this within four questions.

It went up on Mill Street in 1968, came down in 2004 when the lease went, sat in Ed's garage on Fenn Avenue for three years, and went up on the Route 62 building in 2007 after the Historical Society raised about $2,800 to rewire the transformer and replace two sections of tube — the blue in the wing, and part of the L. A good deal of that came in amounts under twenty dollars, in a jar on the counter at Hollis Market.

It is still up. It has outlasted the diner by ten years and it will outlast me.

posts.title: the renewal form
posts.body:
The company that hosts this changed the renewal form in the spring. It now wants me to make an account with a password of a kind I do not have and confirm it somewhere I cannot get to, and I have spent parts of four afternoons on it, and I am sixty-seven and I have decided that is enough afternoons.

The site will stay up as long as the card keeps paying, and the card is an old one that still charges, so it may be up a long while after I stop looking at it.

Everything I said I would put here is here. The menus. The photographs. The booth map. The fire, with the date on it. The pie.

If you want to reach me after this, write to me. I answer letters. I have never once answered an email on the first try.

There is a paper newsletter now, four pages, four times a year, and if you want it you can ask me for it and I will put you on the list. It is not on the internet and it is not going to be.

comments.author: K. Fennimore
comments.body: Marion — the library would like the run of the newsletter for the local collection whenever you are ready. On your terms entirely.

comments.author: marla
comments.body: Four afternoons is three more than I would have given it. Ring me.
